monitor-condition.name: Monitor & Condition Variables
monitor-condition.desc: A monitor combines a mutex + condition variables. A thread can wait() until a condition is true, then be signal()ed.
monitor-condition.q: What is a monitor? How do condition variables work? Why must you always check conditions in a while loop?
monitor-condition.qsub: What is a spurious wakeup? Why can they happen and how do you handle them?
monitor-condition.what: Definition: In a monitor, a thread can wait for a condition inside a lock (wait), and another thread changes the condition and performs notify/signal. The wait atomically releases the lock and sleeps.
monitor-condition.why: Busy-waiting burns CPU; a condition variable puts the thread to sleep, providing efficient coordination (e.g., queue empty/full cases).
cons: Missed signal / lost wakeup ka risk
gotchas: Always check the condition inside a while loop (spurious wakeup)
wait/notify must be called only while holding the lock
notify() wakes only one thread — it may wake the wrong thread
terms: Releases the lock and sleeps; on signal it reacquires the lock and wakes.
Can wake up without a signal.

rwlock.name: Read-Write Lock
rwlock.desc: Multiple readers can hold simultaneously. Only one writer — exclusive. Perfect for read-heavy workloads.
rwlock.q: When would you use a Read-Write Lock over a plain mutex? What are its trade-offs?
rwlock.qsub: What is writer starvation? How do some implementations prevent it?
rwlock.what: Definition: A ReadWriteLock allows multiple readers or a single writer. In a read-heavy workload (95% reads) it provides better throughput than a mutex.
rwlock.why: Serializing reads is wasteful when the data never changes.
gotchas: Upgrading a read lock to a write lock often causes deadlock
In a write-heavy workload, a mutex is faster
Choose based on understanding fair vs non-fair policy
terms: If readers keep arriving, the writer may be blocked.

barrier.name: Barrier & Latch
barrier.desc: Barrier: all threads must reach it before any proceeds. Latch: countdown to zero then releases all waiters.
barrier.q: What is a CyclicBarrier? What is a CountDownLatch? When would you use each?
barrier.qsub: What is the difference between a CountDownLatch and a Semaphore?
barrier.what: Definition: A CyclicBarrier is reusable — after each phase all threads advance together. A CountDownLatch is one-time: the main thread waits until workers call countDown().
barrier.why: In parallel simulations or matrix steps, the next phase needs the complete data from the previous phase.
cons: If one thread gets stuck, everyone gets stuck
gotchas: Latch cannot be reused
If a thread fails in a barrier, a BrokenBarrierException occurs
Perform countDown in a finally block when a worker throws an exception
terms: N threads wait until all have arrived.
When the count reaches 0, it releases everyone once; cannot be reused.
Steps of a parallel algorithm that require synchronization.
where: Waiting for all services to be ready.

// every thread calls b.await() at the end of the phase

deadlock-conditions.name: Four Conditions for Deadlock
deadlock-conditions.desc: Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait. All 4 must hold.
deadlock-conditions.q: What are the four necessary conditions for deadlock? To prevent deadlock, which one would you eliminate?
deadlock-conditions.qsub: Draw a resource allocation graph and show how it demonstrates a deadlock.
deadlock-conditions.what:
Definition: A deadlock occurs when all four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously. Breaking any one prevents a deadlock.

Classic example: Thread 1 holds lock A and requests B; Thread 2 holds B and requests A.
deadlock-conditions.analogy: At an intersection, cars come from all four directions — none can move backward, each waits for the next.
deadlock-conditions.why: Remembering the four helps quickly devise a prevention strategy: each condition suggests a type of fix.
pros: Knowing the conditions enables systematic debugging
cons: Rare at runtime and hard to reproduce
gotchas: All four conditions must be present — break one to solve
After detecting a database deadlock, a transaction is aborted
A thread dump (jstack) shows the cycle
terms: Holding one resource while requesting another.
where: Anything taking locks from both sides.
codeSwap: // Fix: dono mein pehle A phir B (lock ordering)
// Fix: in both, A first and then B (lock ordering)

deadlock-prevention.name: Deadlock Prevention & Avoidance
deadlock-prevention.desc: Prevention: eliminate one Coffman condition. Avoidance: Banker's algorithm. Detection: find cycles in RAG.
deadlock-prevention.q: Compare deadlock prevention, avoidance (Banker's algorithm), and detection. What does each cost?
deadlock-prevention.qsub: Why is the Banker's algorithm rarely used in practice? What do real OSes do instead?
deadlock-prevention.what: Definition: Prevention: lock ordering (circular wait), acquire all locks at once (hold & wait), tryLock+timeout (no preemption). Avoidance decides by looking at the system state. Detection+recovery: if a cycle is found, abort a victim.
deadlock-prevention.why: In production, the practical approach is lock ordering + timeouts + small critical sections.
gotchas: Adding a timeout does not hide the cause — log it
Use random backoff in retries
Banker's algorithm is probably rarely used in real systems
terms: Banker's algorithm — allocate only in a safe state.
Find a cycle in the wait-for graph, then recover.

livelock-starvation.name: Livelock & Starvation
livelock-starvation.desc: Livelock: threads keep responding to each other but make no progress. Starvation: a thread never gets CPU time.
livelock-starvation.q: What is the difference between deadlock, livelock, and starvation? Give a real-world analogy for each.
livelock-starvation.qsub: How do you avoid livelock when implementing retry logic? What is exponential backoff?
livelock-starvation.what: Definition: In a deadlock, threads are blocked; in a livelock they keep running but make no progress. In starvation, a thread is always left behind because of the scheduler/lock policy.
livelock-starvation.analogy: In a corridor, two people keep moving aside for each other, both shifting in the same direction — both are moving, but no one makes forward progress.
livelock-starvation.why: They appear in retry loops and unfair locks; CPU at 100% with zero throughput.
cons: Diagnosing is difficult — CPU appears busy
gotchas: Starvation fix: fair locks, aging
A fixed retry delay keeps both synchronized
Priority inversion is a separate problem
terms: Threads are active but progress is zero.
A thread never gets the resource.
Breaking symmetry with a random wait.
where: On network retries, exponential backoff after a collision.

lock-ordering.name: Lock Ordering & Practical Deadlock Prevention
lock-ordering.desc: Acquire locks in a consistent global order across all threads — the most practical deadlock prevention technique.
lock-ordering.q: How does consistent lock ordering prevent deadlock? What is tryLock with timeout?
lock-ordering.qsub: Show a bank transfer example where two threads deadlock without lock ordering, and how to fix it.
lock-ordering.what: Definition: If every thread acquires locks in the same order (e.g., ascending account ID), circular wait is impossible, so no deadlock.
lock-ordering.why: If a bank transfer A→B and a transfer B→A run simultaneously, a deadlock occurs — ordering fixes it.
cons: Determining order with dynamic locks is difficult
gotchas: Tie-breaker lock for equal id/hash
Locks acquired inside callbacks can break the hidden order
Document the order
terms: A fixed rank for all locks.
Always acquire from lower rank to higher.
where: Rows are updated in sorted order.

thread-pool.name: Thread Pools
thread-pool.desc: Pre-created pool of threads that pick up tasks from a queue. Avoids thread creation overhead, controls resource usage.
thread-pool.q: Why use a thread pool instead of creating a new thread per task? How do you size a thread pool?
thread-pool.qsub: What is the difference between a fixed thread pool and a cached thread pool? What is a work-stealing pool?
thread-pool.what:
Definition: Thread pool keeps a fixed/bounded set of threads that take tasks from a queue. It saves thread-creation cost and provides a concurrency limit.

Sizing: CPU-bound ≈ cores; I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute).
thread-pool.why: An unbounded thread-per-request model can exhaust memory under load and crash.
cons: If sized incorrectly, can cause starvation
If the queue is unbounded, can cause OOM
gotchas: Tasks waiting on a pool inside the same pool can deadlock
An unbounded queue behaves like a memory leak
If shutdown() is forgotten, the JVM does not exit
terms: What to do when the queue is full.

cas-atomic.name: Compare-And-Swap (CAS) & Atomic Operations
cas-atomic.desc: Hardware-supported instruction: atomically compare memory location to expected value and swap if equal. No lock needed.
cas-atomic.q: How does CAS work? Implement an atomic counter using CAS. What is the ABA problem?
cas-atomic.qsub: What is an AtomicReference? How does it differ from a volatile reference?
cas-atomic.what: Definition: CAS is a CPU instruction: if the value in memory equals the expected value, write the new value; otherwise fail. Lock-free counters and stacks are built on it.
cas-atomic.why: Atomic updates without locks reduce contention and eliminate deadlocks.
gotchas: ABA fix: version stamp (AtomicStampedReference)
LongAdder is better under heavy contention
CAS is atomic only for a single variable
terms: If CAS fails, read again and retry.
Value changed from A to B and back to A, which CAS cannot detect.

lock-free.name: Lock-Free & Wait-Free Algorithms
lock-free.desc: Lock-free: system-wide progress guaranteed (at least one thread progresses). Wait-free: every thread progresses.
lock-free.q: What is a lock-free data structure? Why is it hard to implement? When would you use one?
lock-free.qsub: Is lock-free always faster than locked? What overhead does CAS have?
lock-free.what: Definition: Lock-free algorithms use CAS instead of mutexes, so a stalled or suspended thread does not block the others. Wait-free provides the strongest guarantee but is very hard to implement.
lock-free.why: Low-latency systems (trading, kernels) cannot tolerate lock blocking and priority inversion.
cons: Hard to write and to prove correct
gotchas: Lock-free ≠ always faster
Use a proven library first; don’t write your own.
Individual threads can starve.
terms: At least one thread always makes progress.
Each thread finishes in a bounded number of steps.
Finishes if it runs in isolation.

future-promise.name: Futures, Promises & Async/Await
future-promise.desc: A Future represents a value not yet computed. Promise resolves it later. Async/await is syntactic sugar over Futures.
future-promise.q: What is the difference between a Future and a Promise? How does CompletableFuture in Java work?
future-promise.qsub: What is structured concurrency? How does it improve on raw threads and futures?
future-promise.what: Definition: A Future is a pending result that is resolved or rejected later. async/await creates a compiler/runtime state machine that releases the thread at await (does not block).
future-promise.why: Compose asynchronous work (chain, all, race) and handle errors in one place without callback hell.
cons: Error handling and cancellation are subtle
A sequential await accidentally becomes serial
gotchas: await loop runs serially — use Promise.all
Future.get() blocks
An unhandled rejection can crash the process
terms: Placeholder for a value that has not yet arrived.
Writable side that sets the value.

actor-model.name: Actor Model
actor-model.desc: Concurrency without shared state — actors communicate via message passing only. Used in Erlang, Akka, Go channels.
actor-model.q: Explain the Actor model. How does it avoid race conditions without locks?
actor-model.qsub: How do Go goroutines and channels implement the Actor model? What is "Share memory by communicating"?
actor-model.what:
Definition: In the Actor model each actor exclusively owns its state; other actors can only send messages. Messages in a mailbox are processed one at a time, so locks are not needed.

Go’s mantra: “share memory by communicating”.
actor-model.why: Removing shared mutable state eliminates races and naturally scales to distributed systems.
cons: You have to think about message ordering/backpressure
gotchas: An unbounded mailbox can cause OOM
A blocking call inside an actor stalls the entire actor
The request-reply pattern can deadlock
terms: Private state + mailbox; one message at a time.
The parent actor restarts the child on failure (Erlang).
codeSwap: // sirf yahi goroutine c ko chhoota hai

memory-ordering.name: Memory Ordering — sequential consistency, acquire-release, relaxed
memory-ordering.desc: Memory ordering defines the order in which memory operations become visible to other threads. Sequential consistency: all threads see the same order. Acquire-release: release on write, acquire on read (synchronizes). Relaxed: no ordering guarantees (fastest). x86 is mostly TSO (Total Store Order). ARM/POWER are weakly ordered.
memory-ordering.q: What is the difference between sequential consistency and relaxed memory ordering?
memory-ordering.qsub: When would you use acquire-release vs relaxed ordering? How does the Java Memory Model define volatile?
memory-ordering.what: Definition: CPU/compiler instructions reorder. The memory model determines which orderings are guaranteed. SC is the safest and slowest; acquire-release is sufficient for publish patterns; relaxed is for counters.
memory-ordering.why: Lock-free code must be written correctly — a bug due to wrong ordering may appear only on certain architectures.
gotchas: Keep default seq_cst until profiling suggests otherwise
Relaxed does not publish data
x86 is strong, ARM is weak — test on both
terms: All threads see the same global order.
Writes before a release become visible to the acquiring thread.

volatile-keyword.name: volatile keyword — Java, C++, JavaScript differences
volatile-keyword.desc: Java volatile: visibility guarantee (no caching) + happens-before ordering. C++ volatile: prevents compiler optimization (NOT thread-safe, use std::atomic). JavaScript: no volatile (single-threaded). Common misconception: volatile does NOT provide atomicity in Java.
volatile-keyword.q: What does volatile guarantee in Java? Why is it NOT sufficient for thread safety?
volatile-keyword.qsub: What is the difference between volatile in Java and C++? Why doesn't JavaScript need volatile?
volatile-keyword.what: Definition: In Java, a volatile variable's write is seen immediately by all threads and prevents reordering. But volatile int x; x++ is not atomic. In C++, volatile is not for threading (use std::atomic).
volatile-keyword.why: Perfect for flags (stop/ready); wrong tool for counters.
gotchas: volatile count++ is a race
C++ volatile ≠ Java volatile
volatile is required in double-checked singleton
codeSwap: // counter ke liye AtomicInteger, volatile int nahi
// AtomicInteger for the counter, not volatile int

thread-interruption.name: Thread Interruption — cooperative cancellation, InterruptedException, flags
thread-interruption.desc: Thread interruption is cooperative: interrupt sets a flag, the thread must check and respond. Java: Thread.interrupt() + InterruptedException. Python: threading.Event. Go: context.Context with cancel. Never ignore InterruptedException — either rethrow or restore interrupt flag.
thread-interruption.q: How does cooperative thread cancellation work? Why is it preferred over forceful termination?
thread-interruption.qsub: What happens if you catch InterruptedException without rethrowing? How do you implement cancellation in Go with context?
thread-interruption.what: Definition: Forcefully killing a thread is unsafe (locks leak). Therefore interrupt only sets a flag; the thread checks isInterrupted() on blocking calls and exits cleanly.
thread-interruption.why: Cancellation is required for graceful shutdowns and timeouts without leaking resources.
cons: If the code doesn't cooperate, it can't be cancelled
gotchas: Do not swallow InterruptedException — restore the flag
Thread.stop deprecated/unsafe
If a CPU loop doesn't check, interrupt won't work
terms: The thread must check itself to stop.
A blocking call throws this when interrupted.

green-threads.name: Green Threads vs OS Threads — fibers, coroutines, M:N scheduling
green-threads.desc: Green threads (goroutines, Kotlin coroutines, Python asyncio tasks) are multiplexed onto OS threads by a runtime. M:N model: M green threads on N OS threads. Lightweight (~2KB stack for goroutines vs ~1MB for OS threads). Scheduled by runtime, not OS. Blocked green thread yields OS thread.
green-threads.q: What is the difference between green threads and OS threads? How does M:N scheduling work?
green-threads.qsub: How do goroutines differ from Java threads? What is the stack growth strategy for goroutines?
green-threads.what: Definition: Green threads run on the runtime scheduler, not the OS. On blocking I/O the runtime parks the green thread and gives the OS thread to another green thread. Hence hundreds of thousands of concurrent tasks are possible.
green-threads.why: Simple thread-per-request code style, but with scalability similar to async.
cons: CPU-bound work can starve the scheduler
Native blocking calls pin the thread
gotchas: Goroutine leak — ensure an exit path
Virtual threads are not for pooling
Parallelism on CPU-bound work is limited to the number of cores
terms: M green threads on N OS threads.

event-loop-deep.name: Event Loop Deep Dive
event-loop-deep.desc: JS is single-threaded but non-blocking via event loop: call stack + task queue + microtask queue + libuv.
event-loop-deep.q: Explain the JS event loop in detail. What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?
event-loop-deep.qsub: In what order do these run: setTimeout(0), Promise.resolve(), queueMicrotask(), setImmediate()?
event-loop-deep.what: Definition: Loop: when the stack is empty → all microtasks are drained → one macrotask → repeat. Node has libuv phases (timers, poll, check) and process.nextTick runs before microtasks.
event-loop-deep.why: Understanding ordering and blocking — a heavy synchronous function can freeze the entire server.
gotchas: Microtask loop (recursive then) can starve macrotasks
setTimeout(0) does not run immediately
JSON.parse on large payload blocks the loop

worker-threads.name: Worker Threads in Node.js
worker-threads.desc: Node.js Worker Threads enable true parallelism for CPU-bound work. Each worker has its own V8 and event loop.
worker-threads.q: When would you use Worker Threads in Node.js? How do you communicate between them?
worker-threads.qsub: What is SharedArrayBuffer? How does it enable shared memory between workers? What synchronization do you need?
worker-threads.what: Definition: worker_threads remove CPU-heavy work from the main loop. Workers do not share memory (by default) — messages are copied; you can share memory with SharedArrayBuffer.
worker-threads.why: Image resizing, hashing, parsing, etc., do not slow the API on the main thread.
gotchas: Workers are not needed for I/O
Creating a new worker for each request is expensive — use a pool
Functions cannot be sent via postMessage
terms: Data is copied via structured clone.

promises-internals.name: Promise Internals & Error Handling
promises-internals.desc: Promises implement the microtask queue. Unhandled promise rejections can crash Node.js in newer versions.
promises-internals.q: How do Promises work internally? What is Promise chaining vs async/await? What are the error propagation rules?
promises-internals.qsub: What is Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled vs Promise.race vs Promise.any? When do you use each?
promises-internals.what: Definition: Promise callbacks run in the microtask queue. The return value of then resolves the next promise; throwing converts it to a rejection.
promises-internals.why: To understand bugs related to error propagation and ordering.
gotchas: Forgetting to return in then breaks the chain
Without an async function, errors from await are not caught
Promise.all fast-rejects on the first failure — allSettled behaves differently
terms: Each then returns a new promise.
codeSwap: // upar ke kisi bhi step ka error
// the error from any of the steps above

node-cluster.name: Node.js Cluster & Load Balancing
node-cluster.desc: Node Cluster forks multiple worker processes (one per CPU core) sharing the same port — achieves parallelism.
node-cluster.q: How does Node.js Cluster module work? How does the master process distribute connections to workers?
node-cluster.qsub: What is the difference between using Cluster and running multiple Node.js instances behind a load balancer?
node-cluster.what: Definition: The cluster module runs a Node process on each CPU core, all sharing the same port. Memory is not shared, so in-memory sessions/caches are not consistent across workers.
node-cluster.why: Single-threaded Node uses only one core; clustering increases throughput across multiple cores and remaining workers keep running if one crashes.
cons: State is not shared — you need Redis
gotchas: WebSocket requires sticky sessions
In-memory cache is separate per worker
In Kubernetes, use pod replicas instead of cluster
terms: Master forks, workers share the port.
where: Usually one process per container + orchestrator.

gil.name: Python GIL — what it is, why it exists, when it matters
gil.desc: The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. It exists because CPython's reference counting is not thread-safe. It affects CPU-bound code but not I/O-bound code. Removed in Python 3.13+ (free-threaded mode, opt-in).
gil.q: What is the Python GIL? Why does it exist and when does it matter?
gil.qsub: How does the GIL affect CPU-bound vs I/O-bound code? What is the free-threaded mode in Python 3.13?
gil.what: Definition: GIL keeps CPython's reference counting safe. CPU-bound threads do not run in parallel; I/O (sockets, files) or C extensions (NumPy) release the GIL. In Python 3.13+ the free-threaded build is experimental.
gil.why: If you choose the wrong model, speed will not increase even with 8 threads.
gotchas: GIL does not prevent data races (x += 1 is a race)
NumPy/IO release the GIL
Free-threaded Python is not the default yet
terms: In CPython, one thread executes bytecode at a time.
The GIL is released during I/O, so threads can work.

python-threads.name: Threading in Python — threading module, daemon threads, Thread(target=)
python-threads.desc: Python's threading module creates OS threads. Due to the GIL, threads don't help CPU-bound tasks but do help I/O-bound tasks (network, file I/O). Daemon threads die when the main thread exits. join() waits for thread completion.
python-threads.q: When would you use Python threading? Why doesn't it help with CPU-bound work?
python-threads.qsub: What is a daemon thread? How do you use Thread(target=func, args=()) and join()?
python-threads.what: Definition: threading is for I/O-bound concurrency. Thread(target=fn, args=...), start(), join(). Daemon threads do not prevent program exit.
python-threads.why: Overlapping network/file waits is easiest with ThreadPoolExecutor.
gotchas: Do not call f(); pass the function f to Thread(target=f)
Daemon threads are not cleaned up
Exceptions inside a thread die silently
terms: Stops when the main program exits, without waiting.

python-asyncio.name: asyncio — event loop, coroutines, await, asyncio.gather()
python-asyncio.desc: asyncio provides single-threaded concurrency via an event loop. async/await defines coroutines. asyncio.gather() runs multiple coroutines concurrently. asyncio creates tasks that interleave during I/O waits. No GIL contention because single-threaded.
python-asyncio.q: How does asyncio work? What is the difference between asyncio.gather() and asyncio.create_task()?
python-asyncio.qsub: When should you use asyncio vs threading? What is the event loop and how does it schedule coroutines?
python-asyncio.what: Definition: asyncio performs cooperative multitasking on a single thread. When a task reaches await, it suspends and the loop runs another task. A blocking call (time.sleep, requests) stops the entire loop.
python-asyncio.why: Thousands of network connections use less memory—more scalable than threads.
cons: The entire call stack must be async
gotchas: Use asyncio.sleep instead of time.sleep
Use asyncio.to_thread for blocking code
If you forget await, the coroutine never runs
terms: Returns control to the event loop.

python-multiprocessing.name: multiprocessing — bypassing the GIL, shared memory, Process(target=)
python-multiprocessing.desc: multiprocessing spawns separate processes, each with its own Python interpreter and GIL. Bypasses the GIL for CPU-bound work. Communicate via Queue, Pipe, or shared memory (Value, Array, Manager). Overhead of process creation and IPC.
python-multiprocessing.q: How does multiprocessing bypass the GIL? What are the tradeoffs vs threading?
python-multiprocessing.qsub: What is the difference between multiprocessing.Queue and queue.Queue? When would you use shared memory vs message passing?
python-multiprocessing.what: Definition: multiprocessing runs separate processes, so CPU-bound work is truly parallel. Data is transferred via pickling (overhead); shared_memory enables zero-copy sharing.
python-multiprocessing.why: Bypassing the GIL lets you fully utilize multiple cores.
gotchas: Forgetting the if __name__ == '__main__' guard can cause infinite spawning
Lambdas/closures cannot be pickled
For small tasks, overhead can outweigh benefits

producer-consumer.name: Producer-Consumer Problem
producer-consumer.desc: Producers add items to a bounded buffer; consumers remove items. Synchronize to avoid overflow and underflow.
producer-consumer.q: Implement the Producer-Consumer problem using semaphores. Then solve it with a BlockingQueue.
producer-consumer.qsub: How does a message queue system like Kafka implement the producer-consumer pattern at scale?
producer-consumer.what: Definition: Producers add items to the queue, consumers remove them. A bounded buffer slows producers when consumers fall behind (backpressure).
producer-consumer.why: Decoupling and load smoothing — message queues, logging pipelines, worker pools are all built on this.
gotchas: An unbounded queue can fill memory.
Use a poison pill or close signal for shutdown.
If a consumer is slow, the queue fills up.
terms: Consumer waits when empty, producer waits when full.

readers-writers.name: Readers-Writers Problem
readers-writers.desc: Multiple readers can read simultaneously. Writers need exclusive access. Variants: reader-first vs writer-first.
readers-writers.q: Solve the Readers-Writers problem. Which variant prevents starvation and how?
readers-writers.qsub: How does a database implement this pattern for MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)?
readers-writers.what: Definition: Multiple readers can access shared data simultaneously, writer has exclusive access. Variants determine fairness. Solution: ReadWriteLock or semaphores + reader count.
readers-writers.why: Balancing performance and fairness in read-heavy caches/configurations.
gotchas: In reader-preference, the writer can starve.
Reader count updates also require a mutex.
Use a ready-made ReadWriteLock in production.
terms: Readers have priority — writer may starve.
When the writer is waiting, new readers are blocked.

dining-philosophers.name: Dining Philosophers Problem
dining-philosophers.desc: N philosophers alternate eating/thinking, sharing N forks. Demonstrates deadlock and starvation challenges.
dining-philosophers.q: Explain the Dining Philosophers problem. Give two different solutions to avoid deadlock.
dining-philosophers.qsub: What does this problem teach about real-world lock acquisition patterns?
dining-philosophers.what: Definition: Each of the N philosophers needs two forks to eat. If everyone picks up the left fork simultaneously, deadlock occurs. Fixes: fork ordering, a semaphore allowing at most N-1 philosophers at the table, or alternating odd/even ordering.
dining-philosophers.why: A standard model for deadlock/starvation; a common interview example to explain lock ordering.
gotchas: Semaphore(N-1) also works.
Ordering fix does not eliminate starvation.
Real fix = fewer locks
terms: All picked up the left fork → deadlock.
Number the forks and acquire the lower-numbered one first.

thread-safe-singleton.name: Thread-Safe Singleton
thread-safe-singleton.desc: Creating a singleton in a multi-threaded environment — naive lazy initialization is not thread-safe.
thread-safe-singleton.q: What is wrong with double-checked locking for Singleton? How do you implement it correctly?
thread-safe-singleton.qsub: What is the Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom? Why is it the cleanest approach?
thread-safe-singleton.what: Definition: Naive if (inst==null) inst=new X() can create two instances in different threads. Safe options: eager static initialization, holder class, enum, or volatile with double-checked locking.
thread-safe-singleton.why: Reordering can expose a half-constructed object — without volatile, double-checked locking is broken.
gotchas: DCL is broken without volatile.
Different class loaders can create multiple instances.
A DI container is a better option.
terms: First check without lock, then check inside lock.
The simplest safe approach in Java.

cpu-multitasking.name: How the CPU Runs Multiple Threads — Scheduling & Context Switch
cpu-multitasking.desc: A CPU core can only run one thread at a time. The OS scheduler rapidly switches between threads (context switch) — saving one thread's registers and loading another's. This happens so fast (milliseconds) it feels simultaneous. Multi-core CPUs can truly run threads in parallel.
cpu-multitasking.q: How does a single-core CPU appear to run multiple programs at once?
cpu-multitasking.qsub: What is a context switch? What data must be saved and restored? Why does context switching have a cost?
cpu-multitasking.what:
Definition: A core runs only one thread at a time. The scheduler, when the time slice ends (preemption) or when a thread blocks, saves the state (registers, PC) and runs another thread — this is called a context switch.

The switch's work is not directly productive; the cache also gets cold.
cpu-multitasking.analogy: A chef (core) is handling several dishes — a bit of one dish, then notes it and moves to another. It looks like all dishes are being prepared together, but there is only one chef.
cpu-multitasking.why: This creates the illusion that thousands of threads are running together. But more threads mean more switches, which adds overhead.
pros: Multitasking even on a single core
CPU is not wasted during I/O wait
gotchas: Voluntary switch (I/O wait) vs involuntary (time slice expiration) are different things
Thread count far greater than cores slows CPU-bound work
Process switch is more expensive than thread switch (TLB flush)
terms: OS component that decides which thread will run on the CPU next.
Saving the state of the running thread and loading another's.
CPU time allocated to a thread in one go (ms).
where: Thread pool size based on the number of cores.

concurrency-vs-parallelism.name: Concurrency vs Parallelism
concurrency-vs-parallelism.desc: Concurrency: multiple tasks make progress (interleaving). Parallelism: multiple tasks run simultaneously (multi-core).
concurrency-vs-parallelism.q: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism? Give a real-world analogy.
concurrency-vs-parallelism.qsub: Node.js is concurrent but not parallel. Explain what that means. How does Go achieve both?
concurrency-vs-parallelism.what:
Definition: Concurrency is a structure/design property — breaking a program into independent tasks. Parallelism is an execution property — running those tasks on multiple cores simultaneously.

A concurrent program can run correctly on a single core; parallelism requires hardware. The Node.js event loop is concurrent but JavaScript code is not parallel.
concurrency-vs-parallelism.analogy: One cashier handling two lines (alternating) = concurrency. Two cashiers, each handling one line = parallelism.
concurrency-vs-parallelism.why: Concurrency is sufficient for I/O-bound work; parallelism is needed for CPU-bound work. Choosing the wrong tool hurts performance.
pros: Concurrency: simple resource usage, scalable I/O
Parallelism: real speedup on CPU-bound tasks
cons: Parallelism: requires hardware, synchronization, Amdahl's limit
gotchas: Concurrent ≠ parallel — a favorite interview point
Parallelism is always concurrent, but not the reverse
Creating threads does not guarantee parallelism (GIL, single core)
terms: Multiple tasks make progress together — interleaving, even on a single core.
Multiple tasks literally run at the same time — multi-core.
'Concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once; parallelism is about doing lots of things at once.'

race-condition.name: Race Condition
race-condition.desc: When two threads access shared data concurrently and at least one writes — result depends on execution order.
race-condition.q: What is a race condition? Write a code example that demonstrates one.
race-condition.qsub: How do you detect race conditions? What tools exist (ThreadSanitizer, Helgrind)?
race-condition.what:
Definition: When two or more threads access shared data simultaneously and at least one writes, and the outcome depends on timing.

count++ is not atomic: read → add → write. Both threads read 5, both wrote 6 — one update is lost (lost update).
race-condition.why: Race bugs sometimes appear in production but not in tests — money or inventory can become incorrect (double booking, negative balance).
pros: (It's a bug — not a pro) Understanding it leads to better design
gotchas: Check-then-act (if (!exists) create) is a classic race
Data race and race condition are different issues — both can occur
'It works on my machine' — races appear under load
terms: Result depends on the order of thread scheduling.
count++ actually consists of read, add, write — three steps.
A non-deterministic bug that disappears when you debug.
where: Two requests updating the same row simultaneously.

critical-section.name: Critical Section & Mutual Exclusion
critical-section.desc: A code region accessing shared resources. Must be executed by only one thread at a time (mutual exclusion).
critical-section.q: What is a critical section? What are the 4 requirements for a correct mutual exclusion solution?
critical-section.qsub: What is progress and bounded waiting in the context of mutual exclusion?
critical-section.what:
Definition: Critical section is the code region where shared data is accessed. A correct solution has three properties: mutual exclusion, progress (if none is inside, let another enter), bounded waiting (no starvation).

It is protected with a lock or mutex; the smaller the section, the better the concurrency.
critical-section.why: A small critical section = less contention = higher throughput. A large lock makes all threads serial.
cons: Incorrect lock usage can cause deadlock
gotchas: Do not perform slow I/O inside a lock
Lock must be released on exception — try/finally or with
Protecting the same data with different locks does not work
terms: Code portion that touches a shared resource.
Only one thread inside at a time.

design-rate-limiter.name: Design a Thread-Safe Rate Limiter
design-rate-limiter.desc: Token bucket or leaky bucket algorithm implemented with atomic operations or locks for concurrent requests.
design-rate-limiter.q: Design a thread-safe rate limiter that allows 100 req/sec. Implement it in code.
design-rate-limiter.qsub: How would you make it distributed across multiple servers? What data store would you use?
design-rate-limiter.what: Definition: Token bucket: capacity C, refill rate r. Each request takes a token. To make it thread-safe, update (tokens, lastRefill) in a single unit using a lock or CAS.
design-rate-limiter.why: Prevent API abuse; because of concurrency, the limiter must correctly handle its own race conditions.
cons: Shared state in a distributed setup
gotchas: Refill and consume must be atomic
Use a monotonic clock
For multi-node use Redis Lua/atomic

design-cache.name: Design a Thread-Safe LRU Cache
design-cache.desc: LRU cache with concurrent reads/writes — naive locking kills throughput. Segmented locking is the solution.
design-cache.q: Implement a thread-safe LRU cache. How do you handle concurrent reads without a write lock?
design-cache.qsub: How does ConcurrentHashMap use segmented locking? What is the lock striping technique?
design-cache.what: Definition: A global lock kills throughput. Options: segmented/striped locks, or a library like Caffeine; get also reorders the list, so a read lock is not enough.
design-cache.why: Cache is a hot path — contention directly adds latency.
gotchas: Cache stampede: all threads miss on the same key → single-flight
Race between eviction and get
Ensure the cache remains memory-bounded
terms: Load and store on a miss.
codeSwap: // the lock of only that segment

debug-concurrency.name: Debugging Concurrency Bugs
debug-concurrency.desc: Race conditions and deadlocks are non-deterministic — hardest bugs to reproduce and fix.
debug-concurrency.q: How do you debug a deadlock in production? What tools and techniques do you use?
debug-concurrency.qsub: What is a thread dump? How do you analyze one to find a deadlock?
debug-concurrency.what: Definition: Approach: logs with thread-id + timestamp, thread dump (jstack) to find deadlock cycles, TSan/go test -race, stress with randomized delays, and a minimal reproducible case.
debug-concurrency.why: Catching non-deterministic bugs without tools is almost impossible.
gotchas: Logging itself changes timing
Race detector only observes executed paths
Run stress tests even after fixing

web-server-concurrency.name: Concurrency Models for Web Servers
web-server-concurrency.desc: Thread-per-request vs thread pool vs async event-driven. Each has different performance characteristics.
web-server-concurrency.q: Compare multi-threaded vs event-driven concurrency models for a web server. When does each excel?
web-server-concurrency.qsub: Why does Node.js outperform Java thread-per-request for I/O-bound tasks? When does Java win?
web-server-concurrency.what: Definition: Thread-per-request (Apache prefork) is simple but fails at 10k connections (C10K). A pool is resource-bound. Event loop is best for I/O-bound work but blocks CPU-intensive tasks. Hybrid: event loop + worker pool.
web-server-concurrency.why: Choose the model based on workload (I/O vs CPU, number of connections).
gotchas: A blocking call in the event loop stalls everything
Pool size is critical for latency
Little's law: concurrency = rate × latency

what-is-process.name: What is a Process?
what-is-process.desc: A process is a running program. When you open Chrome, the OS creates a process for it — gives it its own memory space, CPU time, and resources. Each process is isolated; one crashing process cannot corrupt another.
what-is-process.q: What is a process? What resources does the OS give to each process?
what-is-process.qsub: Why are processes isolated from each other? What would happen if they shared memory by default?
what-is-process.what:
Definition: Process = a program stored on disk that the OS loads into memory and runs. The OS gives it code, heap, stack, open files, and a PID.

Isolation is enforced by hardware (MMU) — one process cannot directly read/write another's memory. To communicate you need IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory).
what-is-process.analogy: A process is like a separate apartment: its own kitchen, its own electricity meter, its own door. If the neighbor's apartment catches fire, your apartment stays safe.
what-is-process.why: Isolation prevents a buggy program from bringing down the whole system. Browsers run each tab in a separate process so that if one tab crashes, the others remain.
pros: Strong isolation — crashes or memory corruption stay contained
cons: Creation and context switch are expensive
Sharing data via IPC — slow and complex
gotchas: Creating a process is much heavier than a thread
Zombie process: child has exited but the parent did not call wait()
Two processes do not share the same PID, but after fork memory is copy-on-write
terms: Running program instance — its own address space, file descriptors, PID.
Each process is given virtual memory by the OS; it cannot see another process's memory.
Process Control Block — OS record: PID, state, registers, memory maps.
where: Chrome gives each tab/extension a separate process.

what-is-thread.name: What is a Thread?
what-is-thread.desc: A thread is a single sequence of execution inside a process. One process can have many threads — they share the same memory (heap, code, files) but each has its own stack and CPU registers. Threads are "lightweight processes" — much cheaper to create.
what-is-thread.q: What is a thread? How is it different from a process?
what-is-thread.qsub: If threads share memory, what is the danger? Give a simple example of two threads corrupting shared data.
what-is-thread.what:
Definition: A thread is the smallest unit of CPU scheduling. A process can have one or more threads that share code, heap, and file descriptors, but keep separate stacks and program counters.

Because they share memory, threads can exchange data quickly — but this is also the biggest source of bugs.
what-is-thread.analogy: A process is like a restaurant. Threads are its waiters. Everyone shares the same kitchen (heap) and menu, but each waiter has its own order notepad (stack).
what-is-thread.why: An inexpensive way to perform parallel or overlapping work in a single program: keep the UI thread responsive while a background thread handles file/network tasks.
pros: Lighter than a process — creation and switch are cheap
cons: Shared state leads to race conditions and deadlocks
A thread crash can bring down the entire process
gotchas: Calling t.run() does not create a new thread; it is a normal method call
Each thread's stack (≈1 MB) consumes memory — creating thousands of threads is costly
Thread output order is non-deterministic
terms: A sequence of execution within a process — its own stack and registers.
Thread ID; the OS schedules the thread.
All threads in the same process see the same heap/globals.
where: A thread per request or from a thread pool.

// start(), not run() — it creates a new thread

why-threads.name: Why Do We Need Multiple Threads?
why-threads.desc: Two reasons: (1) Responsiveness — while one thread waits for a disk read, another thread can keep the UI running. (2) Performance — on a multi-core CPU, threads can truly run in parallel, speeding up computation. Without threads, a web server could only handle one request at a time.
why-threads.q: Why do we use multiple threads? Give a real example of a program that benefits from threading.
why-threads.qsub: A web server receives 1000 simultaneous requests. How do threads help? What is a thread pool?
why-threads.what:
Definition: Multiple threads have two major benefits: (1) responsiveness — blocking work runs in a separate thread, (2) parallelism — full use of a multi-core CPU.

When one thread is waiting on disk/network, the CPU can be given to another thread instead of sitting idle.
why-threads.why: Today's machines are multi-core; a single thread would use only one core. Servers also have to serve thousands of concurrent clients.
gotchas: Threads accelerate CPU-bound work only when real cores are present (and not in Python because of the GIL)
More threads don’t always mean more speed — beyond a certain point they become slower
Amdahl’s law: the serial portion determines the upper limit of speedup
terms: Slow work runs in the background, the UI/main flow is not blocked.
More work done simultaneously on multi-core.
One thread waits on I/O while another uses the CPU.
where: Fetch other pages while waiting for network.
codeSwap: # Python: I/O-bound kaam threads se overlap
# Python: I/O-bound work overlaps with threads

process-vs-thread.name: Process vs Thread — Memory Model
process-vs-thread.desc: Process: own code, own heap, own stack, own file descriptors — fully isolated. Thread: shared code, shared heap, shared file descriptors — but own stack and own registers. This shared heap is the source of all concurrency bugs.
process-vs-thread.q: Draw the memory layout of a process with 3 threads. What is shared? What is private?
process-vs-thread.qsub: Creating a new process (fork) is expensive — why? Creating a thread is cheap — why?
process-vs-thread.what:
Definition: A process has its own code, heap, stack, and file descriptors (fully isolated). A thread lives inside a process — it shares code, heap, and globals, and only its stack and registers are private.

ProcessThread
MemorySeparateShared heap
CreationHeavyLight
CrashContainedEntire process
Comm.IPCDirect memory
process-vs-thread.why: Design choice: safety requires a process, speed and sharing require a thread. This trade-off is the most common interview question.
cons: Thread: races, a single bug can crash everything
gotchas: Threads have separate stacks — the heap is shared.
After fork(), the child gets a copy-on-write mapping of the parent’s memory.
Interview trap: ‘threads get a separate address space’ — incorrect.
terms: Process separate memory; thread shared memory.
Process switch involves address-space switch + TLB flush; thread switch is cheaper.
Pipes, sockets, or shared memory for communication between processes.

atomicity.name: Atomicity
atomicity.desc: An operation that appears to happen instantaneously — no intermediate state is observable to other threads.
atomicity.q: What does atomic mean? Is i++ atomic? What about a read-modify-write on a 64-bit int on a 32-bit system?
atomicity.qsub: What is the happens-before relationship? How does it relate to the Java Memory Model?
atomicity.what:
Definition: An atomic operation appears to happen in a single instant. Hardware makes some operations (aligned read/write, CAS, fetch-add) atomic; the rest require a lock or an atomic library.

x++, x = x + 1 are normally not atomic.
atomicity.why: The cheapest way to make simple counters and flags safe without using locks is to use atomics.
cons: Locks are needed for multi-variable invariants
gotchas: A combination of atomic ops is not atomic (check-then-act)
Atomicity is not a complete answer for visibility ordering
64-bit long/double are not atomic on some platforms
terms: Operation completes entirely or not at all; no intermediate state is visible.
Cannot be interrupted in the middle.

memory-visibility.name: Memory Visibility & CPU Caches
memory-visibility.desc: CPUs have private caches — writes by one thread may not be visible to others without synchronization.
memory-visibility.q: Why can a thread read stale data even without a race condition? What is the volatile keyword for?
memory-visibility.qsub: What is a memory barrier? What is cache coherence (MESI protocol)?
memory-visibility.what:
Definition: Modern CPUs and compilers reorder/cache. One thread wrote flag = true, but another thread may keep reading the old value from its cache — there is no guarantee without synchronization.

Locks, volatile, and atomics use memory barriers for visibility.
memory-visibility.why: This bug is a 'while(!done)' loop that never terminates — it causes subtle problems.
pros: Predictable concurrent code when you understand the rules
gotchas: Code that runs on x86 may break on ARM
Visibility and atomicity are separate problems
Lock acquisition/release also acts as a memory barrier
terms: Each core's private L1/L2 — writes are not immediately visible to other cores.
When a thread's write becomes visible to another thread.

mutex.name: Mutex (Mutual Exclusion Lock)
mutex.desc: A lock that only one thread can hold at a time. Thread acquires lock, enters critical section, releases lock.
mutex.q: How does a mutex work? What is a spinlock and when is it better than a blocking mutex?
mutex.qsub: What is a reentrant/recursive mutex? What problem does it solve?
mutex.what:
Definition: A mutex protects a critical section. The thread that acquires the lock is the only one that can release it (ownership). If the lock is held, other threads block (sleep).

A reentrant mutex allows the same thread to acquire it repeatedly (it maintains a count).
mutex.why: The most basic tool for keeping shared data correct — other primitives are built on it.
gotchas: Forgetting to unlock = entire system hangs
Do not run callbacks/I/O inside a lock
If a non-reentrant mutex is acquired again by the same thread, it causes self-deadlock
terms: A lock with only one owner at a time.
Same thread can acquire the lock again without deadlock.

semaphore.name: Semaphore
semaphore.desc: A counter-based synchronization primitive. Binary semaphore = mutex. Counting semaphore = limit concurrent access.
semaphore.q: What is a semaphore? How does it differ from a mutex? Implement a bounded buffer using semaphores.
semaphore.qsub: Can a thread release a semaphore it didn't acquire? How is that useful?
semaphore.what:
Definition: A semaphore is a counter. acquire() decreases the counter (blocks if it reaches 0), release() increases it. This allows up to N threads to access a resource.

Difference from a mutex: any thread can release a semaphore, so it is also used for signaling.
semaphore.analogy: A parking lot with 5 slots: when a car arrives, take a slot; if full, wait outside; when a car leaves, a slot becomes free.
semaphore.why: To enforce 'max N concurrent' in connection pools, rate limiting, and producer-consumer buffers.
cons: No ownership — incorrect release can cause bugs
gotchas: If release() is forgotten, permits leak
Semaphore(1) and a mutex are not the same thing
Too many releases can raise the count above its limit
terms: N permits; decreases on acquire, increases on release.
0/1 — like a mutex but without ownership.
